notes:
I found material for every verse, but some kinds of sources are missing. I found nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org, ag.org or pneumareview, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings. Those sections are left out. The only Catholic source I found is catholic.com on v. 14. For the early church I mostly have Chrysostom, a Greek Father whom the Orthodox honour, but he is not an oca.org source.

---

**v. 1**
- Wesley takes "their cities" to mean the other cities of Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Precept Austin suggests the verse really ends chapter 10, since Jesus is now carrying out what He just taught the Twelve. It also quotes Bob Utley: the theme that ties the chapter together is why Jesus' ministry didn't look more successful. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-11-commentary
- Spurgeon (quoted there) says Jesus sent the Twelve ahead and then followed them to back up their message with His own teaching. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-11-commentary

**vv. 2–3: Did John doubt? (views differ)**
- Guzik (Enduring Word): before this, John clearly recognized Jesus as the Messiah. His present doubt may be explained because perhaps he himself had misunderstood the ministry of the Messiah. He may have expected political rescue for Israel, or at least for himself. Guzik also says John may have treated "the Coming One" (the prophet of Deut 18:15) as a different figure from the Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
- Precept Austin also speaks of John's doubts. Quoting a Ryrie note, it adds that John still had disciples, and some kept to his teaching after Pentecost (Acts 19:1–6). https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-11-commentary
- **Chrysostom (early church):** John did not doubt at all. His own disciples were jealous of Jesus, so he sent them to learn the difference between Jesus and himself. neither did he send as being himself in doubt, nor did he ask in ignorance. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf110/npnf110.iii.XXXVI.html
- **Wesley (Methodist)** agrees with Chrysostom: John sent them not because he doubted himself; but to confirm their faith (this quote comes from the fetched Wesley page). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm

**v. 4**
- Wesley: what they heard and saw was stronger proof than any bare claim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Chrysostom: Jesus answered with healings because people trust deeds more than words. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf110/npnf110.iii.XXXVI.html
- Precept Austin (KJV "show John again"): Jesus gave no new evidence, only a review of what they had already seen, which shows the value of going over things again. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-11-commentary

**v. 5**
- Wesley calls the gospel preached to the poor the greatest mercy of all and points to Isa 29:18 and 35:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Utley (quoted at Precept Austin): Isaiah listed signs for recognising the Messiah, and these are the very acts recorded in chapters 8–9. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-11-commentary

**v. 6**
- Guzik: Jesus' focus offended people who wanted freedom from Rome, but those who aren't offended by a Messiah they didn't expect are blessed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/

**vv. 7–8**
- Wesley: nothing could shake John's witness. "Soft clothing" points to a flattering courtier, who belongs in a palace, not the wilderness. He also thinks Jesus waited until John's disciples had left before praising John. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Guzik: John was steady like no reed, and disciplined rather than in love with comfort. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
- Matthew Henry: many went out of curiosity, not conscience, and hearers will have to give an account of why they came. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/matthew/11.htm

**vv. 9–10**
- Wesley: John was "more than a prophet" because the other prophets pointed to Christ from far off, while John was His immediate forerunner (Mal 3:1). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Guzik: John alone had the job of being the Messiah's herald. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
- Precept Austin: the Greek tense of "it is written" means the writing still stands. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-11-commentary
- Henry: Scripture still speaks even though its writers are dead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/matthew/11.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: Though John was great, he was not born again under the New Covenant. This is because he lived and died before the completion of Jesus' work at the cross and empty tomb. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
- Wesley quotes an ancient writer: being baptised into Christ's death is greater than being perfect under the law. The least Christian, born again, is greater than anyone who has only the law's righteousness, and knows Christ more fully than John could. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Precept Austin: "born of women" is an idiom for any human. It adds that John was the friend of the bridegroom, while the disciples became the bride (John 3:29). https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-11-commentary

**v. 12: The most disputed verse (traditions really differ)**
- **"Eager seekers" reading (older commentators and many evangelicals):**
  - Ellicott: the "violent" are people of eager zeal grabbing the kingdom's peace and pardon. He sees no hostile meaning here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/11-12.htm
  - Barnes compares the crowds pressing in to soldiers storming a city. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/11-12.html
  - GotQuestions takes the same view. https://www.gotquestions.org/kingdom-God-suffers-violence.html
  - Wesley (Methodist): people rush into the kingdom like soldiers taking a city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
  - Henry: the kingdom calls for a "holy violence" of self-denial and striving. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/11-12.html
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** this is the plain teaching of the text. A person seeking salvation must be fiercely in earnest, and this earnestness continues after conversion as love for Christ. He links this to the Spirit's work, not human merit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/matthew-11.html
- **Reformed (Ligonier, David Briones):** the word for "the violent" is always negative, so it means the kingdom's enemies. The kingdom is under attack, not being entered eagerly. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/violent-take-it-force
- **Lutheran (LCMS Witness):** it rejects the old NIV reading ("forcefully advancing… forceful men lay hold of it"). The verse is not about our activity, it's about what the kingdom suffers. https://witness.lcms.org/2025/the-kingdom-of-heaven-suffers-violence/
- **Other readings:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary notes Weiss's view that Jesus is criticising political attempts to force the kingdom into being. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/11-12.htm
  - R. Tuck: Jesus is correcting John's wish for more force, not praising force. https://biblehub.com/sermons/matthew/11-12.htm
  - F.F. Bruce (via Precept Austin): despite John's arrest, the kingdom has kept advancing. Violent men may try armed force, but that is not how it wins. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-11-commentary
  - Coffman: some tried to enter early, before the gates opened at Pentecost. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/11-12.html
- **Modern-scholarly flavour:** Barclay says the line sounds more like Matthew's own comment on the persecution of his day than a saying of Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/11-12.html

**v. 13**
- Wesley: the Law and Prophets foretold from far off what is now happening. With John the old order ended and the new began. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Guzik: Jesus saw an era closing with John. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/

**v. 14: Is John Elijah?**
- Most sources agree: John is Elijah "in spirit and power" (Luke 1:17), not literally Elijah. That is why John could deny being Elijah (John 1:21).
  - Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
  - Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/11-14.html
  - GotQuestions: https://www.gotquestions.org/John-Baptist-Elijah.html
- Calvin: John's office doesn't depend on people accepting him. "If you are willing" rebukes their ingratitude. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/11-14.html
- **Future Elijah (differing views):**
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel): John fulfilled the first coming, but Elijah himself will come before Christ returns. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/11-14.html
  - Constable (dispensational): whether John counted as Elijah depended on Israel repenting. Since Israel rejected Jesus, Mal 4:5–6 is still unfulfilled. He notes that amillennialists and some premillennialists disagree. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/11-14.html
- **Catholic:** John has Elijah's role as a "type" of Elijah. He is not literally the person Elijah. https://www.catholic.com/qa/why-does-john-the-baptist-deny-he-is-elijah
- Origen (on catholic.com) rejects reading this verse as reincarnation: the "spirit and power" of Elijah are meant, not his soul. https://www.catholic.com/tract/reincarnation%20quotes%20by%20church%20fathers%20against%20reincarnation

**v. 15**
- Wesley: a proverbial call for the deepest attention. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Spurgeon: blessing comes through the listening ear. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-11-commentary

**vv. 16–17**
- Wesley: they are like sulky children who won't be pleased by anything. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Guzik: people determined to criticise will always find something. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/

**vv. 18–19**
- Wesley: John lived strictly like Elijah, while Jesus mixed freely with people. "Wisdom is justified" means His wisdom is recognised by the truly wise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Guzik: look at what each of them actually did. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
- Henry: "friend of sinners" is in fact Christ's eternal praise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/matthew/11.htm

**vv. 20–24**
- Wesley: Jesus had never rebuked these towns before. The "woes" are not curses but a sad, compassionate statement of the misery they were bringing on themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Guzik: greater light brings greater responsibility, and "more tolerable" implies degrees of judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
- Henry: refusing to repent is the great damning sin of people who have heard the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/matthew/11.htm
- Spurgeon on Sodom: those who sinned against the light will be punished more. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-11-commentary
- Wesley on v. 23: "exalted to heaven" means highly honoured by His presence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm

**vv. 25–26: Election and revelation (traditions differ)**
- Guzik: Jesus rejoiced that God chose unlikely people, against a background of growing rejection. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
- **Gill (Calvinist Baptist):** the difference between people is not due to their intelligence, worth or future response. It is due to the good will and pleasure of God only. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/matthew/11-26.html
- **Expositor's Bible:** Jesus gives thanks because of the hiding, not merely in spite of it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/matthew-11.html
- **Wesley (Methodist):** a softer reading. God hast suffered these things to be hid from the self-wise and showed them to the humble. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Barnes: "the wise" means those wise in their own eyes. The only satisfactory reason given is that it pleased God. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/matthew/11-26.html
- Pulpit Commentary: even the most guileless heart can't see spiritual truth unless God draws back the veil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/11-25.htm

**v. 27**
- Guzik: a stunning claim to divine authority. There are no secrets between the Father and the Son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
- Wesley: no one can know God by natural reason, only those to whom the Son reveals Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm

**v. 28**
- Spurgeon (in Guzik): come first to the personal Saviour, not to a doctrine, ceremony or minister. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
- Carson (in Guzik): "labour" means burdens we take on ourselves, and "heavy laden" means burdens others put on us (compare 23:4). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
- Precept Austin: no one comes until they feel their need, and the invitation leaves no one out. In context the "rest" is salvation, but believers should keep entering it as they grow. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew_1128-30_commentary
- **Wesley (Methodist distinctive):** the rest is from sin's guilt through justification and from sin's power through sanctification. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm

**v. 29**
- Guzik: we come as learners, not only to receive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-11/
- JFB: Christ invites us to follow the same path of self-giving that gave Him rest. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/matthew-11.html
- Wesley: taking the yoke means believing in Christ as prophet, priest and king. If you find no rest, the fault is in you, not the yoke. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm

**v. 30**
- Guzik: the yoke is light because He carries it with us, fitted like a well-made ox-yoke. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/easy-yoke-light-burden/
- Wesley: "easy" could be rendered gracious or kind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/11.htm
- Precept Austin: "light" (elaphros) means not oppressive, easy to bear. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew_1128-30_commentary
